title: Fix Bitter Home Espresso in Three Steps
audience: Complete beginners anywhere in the world who just bought their first espresso machine.
brief: Teach three fixes for bitter home espresso: grind, dose and water temperature. Goal: viewers join the free newsletter at coffeelab.example/newsletter to get the recipe card.

issues.description: The opening spends about 20 seconds on greetings and throat-clearing and never states what the viewer will get; the actual promise only arrives after the intro.
Dense barista jargon (channeling, puck prep, TDS, brew ratio, extraction yield, distribution tool) is used with no explanation for a beginner audience.
A roughly 35-second story about a cousin's wedding in Lisbon has no connection to fixing espresso and stalls the tutorial.
Gives temperature only in Fahrenheit and assumes US retailers (Walmart, Target) and a US cultural reference for a worldwide audience.
The brief's goal is newsletter sign-ups, but the video ends with 'Thanks, bye' and never mentions the newsletter or recipe card.

lines.text: Hey guys, welcome back to the channel, it's me again.
So, um, today I thought we could maybe talk about a few things related to coffee, and, yeah, we'll just see where it goes.
Before we start, a quick hello to everybody who is new here, and also to everyone who isn't new here.
Home espresso tastes bitter for three reasons, and each one takes about a minute to fix.
Reason one: your grind is wrong.
A good shot of espresso takes about twenty-five to thirty seconds to pour.
If it gushes out in ten seconds, grind finer.
If it drips for forty seconds, grind coarser.
Now, to dial in properly, watch for channeling in the puck, since uneven extraction produces a high TDS with sour acidity on the front end.
If your brew ratio is off, adjust your puck prep, distribution tool and tamp pressure until you hit the target extraction yield.
Reason two: the amount of coffee in the basket.
Weigh your coffee instead of guessing.
For most home machines, eighteen grams in the basket is a great starting point.
Funny enough, this reminds me of last summer, when my cousin got married in Lisbon.
Her wedding was in this old convent, and the caterer had the strangest espresso cart I have ever seen.
It had a little brass bell, and every time somebody ordered, he rang it twice.
My cousin's husband rang it about forty times just to annoy him.
I took so many photos of that cart, and one day I'll post them on my second channel.
My other cousin, who lives in Porto, says Lisbon is overrated, which I think is wrong, because the trams alone are worth the trip.
Okay, back to coffee.
Reason three: water temperature.
Aim for two hundred degrees Fahrenheit, which any barista in the States will tell you is the sweet spot.
And if you need a thermometer or a kitchen scale, just grab one at Walmart or Target on your way home.
So that's it: grind, dose and temperature.
Try them one at a time, and taste the difference after each change.
And that's all I've got.
Thanks, bye.
